one_liner: Header-only C++17 JSON/CBOR/MsgPack/UBJSON value-and-events library; beat nlohmann 2.0.3 in a 2016 run, mainly on number-heavy JSON.
what_it_does: taoJSON gives you a generic tao::json::value (a std::variant over int64, uint64, double, std::string, binary, std::vector and std::map) plus an Events interface that connects parsers, serialisers and transformers for JSON, JAXN (relaxed JSON), CBOR, MsgPack and UBJSON. Type and binding traits convert values or event streams to and from your own C++ types, and a parts parser can read straight into user types without building a DOM. It also implements JSON Pointer and JSON Patch. The API is its own (from_string, to_string, value::at, as<T>), not nlohmann-compatible. contrib/nlohmann.cpp converts events to and from nlohmann's types.
how_it_is_fast: The JSON grammar is a PEGTL parsing-expression grammar compiled through templates into a recursive-descent parser that sends events directly to a consumer, with no separate tokenizer. Integers of 20 digits or fewer take a strtoull fast path; other numbers go through the bundled V8 double-conversion Strtod for correctly rounded doubles. Output writes integers with jeaiii itoa and doubles with Ryu shortest round-trip printing. The design notes say it 'strives for speed through minimalism (rather than complicated optimisations)': it has no SIMD, no arena allocator, and strings are UTF-8-validated one code point at a time. That explains why it beat an old nlohmann on numbers but trails RapidJSON by about 5x.
when_to_use: You want one value model and one events pipeline across JSON, JAXN, CBOR, MsgPack and UBJSON, with transformers, JSON Pointer and JSON Patch in a header-only C++17 library
Correctness matters more than throughput: it has a 100% Native JSON Benchmark conformance score, correctly rounded double parsing and shortest round-trip double printing

Your documents are number-heavy (coordinates, telemetry), which is the only workload where a measured win over nlohmann exists: 2.2x parse and 3.5x stringify on canada.json against nlohmann 2.0.3 in 2016
You want to bind JSON directly to C++ structs through binding traits or the parts parser instead of walking a DOM
Your project already uses PEGTL and you want consistent error messages with source positions
when_not_to_use: Raw parse or serialise speed is the goal: in the same 2016 suite it parsed 5.2x slower than RapidJSON, and in a 2019 Boost.JSON table (no harness published) it was about 9-13x slower than RapidJSON. simdjson, yyjson or glaze are the speed picks
Your documents are string-heavy: it was slightly slower than nlohmann 2.0.3 on citm_catalog parse (10.27 vs 9.88 ms), and it was 4-5x slower than nlohmann in the 2019 Boost.JSON table
Input is untrusted and may be deeply nested: no nesting-depth limit is visible in the grammar or parse entry points, and issue #121 reported a stack overflow on a malformed file
Your inputs contain duplicate keys or you must preserve key order: objects are a sorted std::map, and DOM parsing throws on a duplicate key

Memory or binary size is tight: in 2016 its parse peak memory was 1.6-1.9x nlohmann's and its test binary was 105,256 vs 42,132 bytes (derived from page data). It is also still pre-1.0 (1.0.0-beta.11), and the README says parts of the API may change

integration.dependencies: PEGTL 3.x (CMake asks for 3.1.0 or later and falls back to the external/PEGTL git submodule); the double-conversion, Ryu and jeaiii itoa code is bundled in include/tao/json/external
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMake 3.10+ for the bundled build; Conan package taocpp-json)
integration.platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux and Android in CI; commits add loongarch64 (2024) and riscv64 (2026) support; non-Windows builds need the compiler to define __BYTE_ORDER__
integration.thread_safety: not documented (the value is a plain std::variant over STL containers, and no locking appears in basic_value.hpp)

gotchas: Parsing into a value throws std::runtime_error on a duplicate object key (set_value::member calls try_emplace, then throw_duplicate_key_exception). Objects are std::map<std::string, value, std::less<>>, so serialising emits keys in sorted order rather than input order.

The JSON grammar recurses (value, array, element, value) under PEGTL's default control and has no nesting-depth guard in grammar.hpp, action.hpp, errors.hpp or from_input.hpp. Issue #121 (2022, stack overflow from from_file on a malformed file) is closed with no visible fix comment, so guard untrusted input yourself.

The record's Boost.JSON caveat is wrong. At boostorg/json commit 8102e7b, doc/qbk/benchmarks.qbk (added in e73d488, 2019-10-23) lists tao-json and nlohmann in the same table on the same inputs: 2056-2178 ms vs 491-495 ms for 55,952,763 bytes and 22952-23265 ms vs 4195-4320 ms for 488,889,121 bytes. That makes tao-json about 4.2-5.5x slower than nlohmann (derived from page data). No tao-json harness exists in any of the ten bench/bench.cpp versions checked, and no hardware or compiler is stated, so this is unreproducible directional evidence. It still contradicts the 2016 win.

nativejson-benchmark's harness (src/tests/taocpptest.cpp on master) calls tao::json::sax::from_string, sax::from_value and sax::to_stream, which no longer exist (the current tree uses tao::json::events). The 2016 numbers cannot be re-run against today's taoJSON without porting the harness. That suite also reports best-of-10 timings with DOM destruction excluded.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over jsoncons or nlohmann when you specifically want its events and transformer architecture, JAXN support and strict conformance; jsoncons covers the same binary formats and has measured 2.1x read and 3.9x write wins over nlohmann. For speed, pick glaze, yyjson or simdjson; taoJSON was never close to RapidJSON.
verified_claims_summary: In nativejson-benchmark's 2016-09-09 sample run (clang 7.0 64-bit, premake 'Full' optimisation with -march=native, Core i7-4980HQ, macOS), the 2016 taoJSON development commit d380c63 parsed canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json into a DOM in 41.2 ms total vs 72.5 ms for nlohmann 2.0.3 (1.8x) and stringified them in 31.0 vs 87.7 ms (2.8x). Per file, the parse win is 2.2x on canada.json, 1.3x on twitter.json and 0.96x (slower) on citm_catalog.json; excluding canada.json, the totals are 1.08x for parse and 1.21x for stringify (derived from page data).
status_note: Maintained but slow-moving: the last commit, a riscv64 port merged on 2026-09-20, follows mostly CI and build fixes since 2023. It is still pre-1.0 (1.0.0-beta.11), MIT-licensed, header-only and easy to vendor with PEGTL. The only reproducible speed evidence is the 2016 run against nlohmann 2.0.3, and an independent but unreproducible 2019 Boost.JSON table shows it 4-5x slower than nlohmann, so treat it as a conformance and flexibility choice, not a speed one.
